_comment: PARTY-BLIND verdict criteria — how to judge ANY policy's effect on a single fundamental, with no reference to which party proposed it. v6 = the rebalanced (value-neutral) frame: 15 outcomes spanning every major tradition's goods, so a policy's intended benefit can register as a benefit, not only its costs. A verdict is a pure function of (policy_text, grounding, criteria[fundamental]).
shared: Judge ONLY this policy's marginal, real-world effect on THIS fundamental for ordinary people, on the evidence given. Be party-blind: the prompt does not name the party and your verdict must not depend on who proposed it — the identical policy text must earn the identical verdict whoever tables it. 'improves'/'worsens' = the direction of effect on the fundamental; 'mixed' = real upsides AND downsides that both land (you are confident about both); 'too-uncertain' = credible non-fringe analysts genuinely disagree or the deciding parameter spans a range no honest number resolves (requires a real crux + estimate range, never a lazy hedge); 'negligible' = no material effect. magnitude = how big (evidence-led, don't inflate); time_horizon = when felt. Keep the three evidence tiers separate (stated / measurable baseline / projected forecast). CITATION DISCIPLINE: base every factual claim on the grounded sources PROVIDED to you; cite only sources that actually appear in that provided research, with their publisher and source_type stated correctly; never invent a source, never cite one you were not given, never mislabel a publisher or type. If you cannot support a claim from the provided sources, drop it. LEAN WITH THE EVIDENCE, DON'T MANUFACTURE BALANCE: choose 'mixed' or 'too-uncertain' ONLY when BOTH sides are genuinely supported by the cited evidence. If the evidence points one way and the only counter-argument is your own reasoning unsupported by a cited source, lean with the evidence — do NOT inflate an ungrounded counter-consideration into false balance. JUDGE EFFECTS, NOT MOTIVES: never infer intent from a policy's framing or political language; do not call a policy ideological/cynical/discriminatory-in-intent — score only the modelled effect. Handle advocacy/campaign sources symmetrically whether they support or oppose the policy.

fundamentals.O1: Affordable housing — can people afford a decent home, to rent or buy, near their life? Weigh: supply (homes actually built/permitted, not just targets), affordability for lower incomes (not just averages), rents and house prices, social/affordable tenure, security of tenure. Watch for: pledges that raise supply but not affordability, or help buyers while shrinking social stock.
fundamentals.O2: Cost of living — can people afford the essentials: food, energy, bills? Weigh: effect on prices and on take-home/disposable income for ordinary and lower-income households, energy and food costs, tax thresholds and benefits in real terms. Distinguish immediate relief from long-run effects. (The absolute TAX burden is O11; the rich-poor GAP is O14 — judge cost of essentials here.)
fundamentals.O3: Healthcare — can people get treated when they need it? Weigh: access and waiting times, capacity (staff, beds, GP/dental access), funding adequacy vs demand, social care interface. Distinguish stated funding from delivered capacity.
fundamentals.O4: Good work & fair pay — can people earn a decent, secure living? Weigh: pay levels and security, employment rights, job creation/quality, conditions, and effects on different kinds of workers. Watch trade-offs between protections and hiring. This is the DISTRIBUTIONAL/quality side of the labour market — aggregate growth and opportunity are O13.
fundamentals.O5: Crime, justice & national security — are streets safe, the country secure, does justice work? Weigh: crime and its drivers, policing and prevention, the justice system (courts, sentencing, victims), national security and defence. This is the PROTECTIVE good ONLY: judge the effect on safety, order, justice and security. Do NOT net in the civil-liberty COST of enforcement (surveillance, stop-and-search, detention, speech or protest limits) — that is scored separately on O10. A measure can IMPROVE O5 and WORSEN O10 at the same time; judge only the safety effect here.
fundamentals.O6: Clean environment & nature — is the air, water, climate and natural world liveable, now and for the future? Weigh: emissions and climate, air and water quality, biodiversity and nature, and the credible pathway/trade-offs (cost, speed, who bears it). DUAL HORIZON: weigh BOTH near-term and long-term (~10yr+) effects; where they diverge (near-term cost but durable long-term gain, or the reverse), say so and judge on the balance, not just the immediate. Government/modelled climate projections are projected-tier, never measured.
fundamentals.O7: Education & opportunity — can children get a good education and can adults get the skills to get on? Weigh: school standards and funding, attainment and the gap for poorer pupils, early years, FE/skills/apprenticeships, access to higher education.
fundamentals.O8: Security in later life — a dignified retirement and care when old? Weigh: pensions (state and private) and their real value, social care funding and access, support for carers, security against later-life poverty.
fundamentals.O9: Equal treatment & democratic rights — are people treated equally and fairly, with a fair say and due process? STRICT scope: equal treatment and anti-discrimination, protection of minorities, voting and democratic rights, due process and the rule of law. This is the EQUAL-TREATMENT / legal-status half of rights. Individual liberty, free speech, privacy and bodily autonomy are NOT here — they are O10. These two can conflict (a measure can advance equal treatment here while restricting liberty on O10) — score each independently. NOT general governance, economic regulation, public services, transport, or welfare.
fundamentals.O10: Personal liberty & free speech — are people free from undue state control over their speech, bodies and choices? Scope: freedom of expression and protest, privacy and freedom from surveillance, bodily autonomy, freedom from state coercion (mandates, compulsory ID/licensing), and property rights against arbitrary interference. A policy that WITHDRAWS state coercion or expands speech/privacy IMPROVES this; new surveillance, criminalising speech/protest, mandates or detention powers WORSEN it — even where the same policy improves safety (O5) or equal treatment (O9). Judge the liberty effect on its own. Liberty is not a left or right good; score the effect, not the politics.
fundamentals.O11: Tax & the money you keep — how much of what people earn do they keep? Weigh: the effect on household tax burden and take-home pay, marginal and average rates, and the DISTRIBUTION of who gains or loses. A tax cut that raises take-home pay IMPROVES this; a tax rise WORSENS it — judged on the money-in-pocket effect ONLY. Whether the revenue forgone or raised is wise is NOT judged here: the public-services effect lands on O3/O7/O8 and sustainability on O12. Party-blind and evidence-led (IFS/OBR distributional analysis); say who is affected, don't assume only the average household.
fundamentals.O12: Public finances & the next generation — do the sums add up, or is the bill passed on? Weigh: sustainability of the debt path, the debt-interest burden, whether spending is funded or borrowed, and whether borrowing finances consumption or productive investment. STAY MACRO-NEUTRAL — do NOT assume 'deficits are bad' or 'austerity is good': borrowing to invest can IMPROVE long-run sustainability by raising future capacity, while unfunded giveaways (spending OR tax cuts) can WORSEN it. Judge on the evidence (OBR/IFS), never on a prior about the right size of the state. DUAL HORIZON: weigh near-term and long-term (~10yr+) debt-path effects separately where they diverge. Both unfunded spending and unfunded tax cuts can score 'worsens' here — symmetrically.
fundamentals.O13: Prosperity & living standards — is the economy growing, with real opportunities to get on? Weigh: real living standards, productivity and business investment, economic opportunity and mobility, business dynamism and formation. NOT raw GDP for its own sake — a policy that trades near-term output for durable long-term living-standard gains (infrastructure, skills, clean energy) must not be marked down as if growth were the only good. DUAL HORIZON: assess near-term AND long-term (~10yr+) effects on living standards separately where they diverge. Distinct from O4 (this is the AGGREGATE/supply side and opportunity; O4 is wage levels, security, job quality) and from O2 (prices households face). Party-blind, evidence-led.
fundamentals.O14: Inequality & fair shares — is the gap between the richest and the rest widening or narrowing? Weigh: income and wealth inequality, the gap between top and bottom, regional inequality, and who gains and who pays. A policy that narrows the gap IMPROVES this; one that widens it WORSENS it — judged on the DISTRIBUTION of gains and losses, party-blind and evidence-led. Distinct from O11 (the absolute tax burden) and O2 (absolute living costs): a policy can cut average taxes (improve O11) while widening the gap (worsen O14). Whether a narrower gap is desirable is the reader's value; judge only the direction of effect on the gap.
fundamentals.O15: Community cohesion & belonging — do people feel part of a community they can trust and belong to? Weigh: social trust, civic participation and volunteering, integration vs segregation, inter-group relations and hate-crime, loneliness and sense of belonging. Evidence-led (social-trust surveys, segregation and participation data). The valence is broadly uncontested (more trust and belonging is widely held to be good), but judge the effect from the EVIDENCE and the mechanism — never infer a cohesion effect from a policy's political framing.
